## "So — is it a breach?"

Your Quality Analyst (QA) is in your office with the systems administrator, and for once
neither of them opens with a finding. They open with the question everyone's been circling
for three modules: "Is it a breach, or isn't it?"

You can tell them exactly what's settled and exactly what isn't. `the-hipaa-privacy-rule`
settled that pulling the Brookfield extract was a permitted health care operations use, no
authorization needed — but that the extract carried three fields (donor name, date of birth,
lifetime donation count) it didn't need, a minimum-necessary gap, logged and separate.
`security-rule-safeguards-and-part-11` settled that encryption of e-PHI (protected health
information in electronic form) is an Addressable specification, that Lakeshore's
full-disk-encryption policy was a sound response to that specification — and that none of
that matters for this one device, because a device-management migration left its
encryption-status field reading "not reported," and nobody can confirm encryption was
actually running on it when it went missing.

None of that answers today's question. Whether pulling the extract was permitted is a
Privacy Rule question. Whether the encryption policy was sound is a Security Rule question.
Whether this is a reportable **breach** is a third, completely different question, governed
by its own subpart with its own definitions, and it has exactly one test: 164.402's
four-factor risk assessment. That's today's job — run the actual test, against the actual
facts, and see where it lands. Not where you'd like it to land. Where it actually lands.

## Why this rule exists, and the ITSM bridge

Every other module in this course has been about prevention and permission — who's allowed to
see PHI, what has to stand between it and an attacker. This module is about what happens after
prevention has already failed, or might have. The failure mode the Breach Notification Rule
exists to prevent isn't the loss itself — that's already happened by the time this rule
engages. It's the second failure: an organization that knows its data may be compromised and
says nothing, leaving every affected person unable to watch their own accounts, freeze their
own credit, or ask their own questions, because they never found out there was anything to
watch for.

You already run the ITSM (IT Service Management) version of this discipline, and you've
probably run it under pressure. A major incident doesn't end when the system is restored — it
triggers a separate obligation: a post-incident review, a customer notification if an SLA
(service level agreement) or a data-handling commitment was breached, a root-cause record for
the next change advisory board. The breach-notification rule is that same obligation, except
the "customer" is 212 donors who never signed an SLA, the "post-incident review" is a
federally defined four-factor test with a specific legal standard, and the notification clock
runs in calendar days with no extension for a busy quarter. The underlying logic is identical
to major incident management: contain, assess impact, notify the people affected, notify the
authority that tracks the pattern across the industry. What's different is that HIPAA (Health
Insurance Portability and Accountability Act) writes the assessment test and the clock into
regulation instead of leaving them to your own incident-management policy.

## The rule in plain English

Start with the question that decides everything else: did an impermissible use, access,
acquisition, or disclosure of PHI happen at all, and if so, is it something more than a
near-miss the rule itself excuses? 164.402 answers both halves. First, it defines "breach" —
broadly, as an impermissible acquisition, access, use, or disclosure that compromises
security or privacy — and then carves out three narrow exclusions for honest, contained
internal mistakes that never actually implicate security (a workforce member's good-faith,
in-scope slip; an inadvertent disclosure between two people both already authorized to see
PHI at the same organization; a disclosure to someone who, in good faith, almost certainly
couldn't have retained what they briefly saw).

Second — and this is the part that decides the laptop's fate — 164.402(2) sets a
**presumption**. An impermissible use or disclosure that doesn't fall into one of those three
exclusions is **presumed to be a breach**, full stop, unless the covered entity affirmatively
demonstrates a low probability that the PHI was compromised. That's not a neutral coin flip.
The organization carries the burden, and it carries it by running a specific four-factor risk
assessment: (1) the nature and extent of the PHI involved, including re-identification
likelihood; (2) who the unauthorized person was, or who the disclosure went to; (3) whether
the PHI was actually acquired or viewed; and (4) the extent to which the risk has been
mitigated. Rebut the presumption on all four factors credibly, and you may conclude no breach
occurred. Fail to rebut it, and the incident is a breach, with everything 164.404, 164.406,
and 164.408 demand.

One more definition matters before any of this engages at all: 164.402 only reaches
**unsecured** PHI — PHI not rendered unusable, unreadable, or indecipherable to an
unauthorized person through an HHS (Department of Health and Human Services)-specified
technology or method. If the extract had been confirmed encrypted to that standard, the
analysis would likely stop here: properly secured PHI generally isn't "unsecured protected
health information" in the first place, and the whole four-factor test might never need to
run. That's exactly why module 3's unresolved encryption-verification gap matters so much to
this module — it's the fact that would have let this incident exit at the front door instead
of going through all four factors.

## Citation decoder

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| 45 CFR 164.402 | "One-sixty-four point four-oh-two" | **Regulation.** Defines "breach," its three narrow exclusions, the presumption-of-breach-unless-rebutted standard, the four-factor risk assessment, and "unsecured protected health information." | The entire test this module runs against the Brookfield laptop. |
| 45 CFR 164.404 | "Four-oh-four" | **Regulation.** Notification to individuals: the 60-calendar-day clock from discovery, and the five required content elements. | What Lakeshore owes the ~212 donors if the breach presumption isn't rebutted. |
| 45 CFR 164.406 | "Four-oh-six" | **Regulation.** Media notification — triggered only when a breach affects more than 500 residents of a State or jurisdiction. | Not triggered here — the extract covers roughly 212 donors, well under the threshold. |
| 45 CFR 164.408 | "Four-oh-eight" | **Regulation.** Notification to the HHS Secretary — a different clock and format for breaches of 500+ individuals versus fewer than 500. | The under-500 annual-log pathway, 164.408(c), is this incident's applicable track if the presumption holds. |
| 45 CFR 164.414 | "Four-fourteen" | **Regulation.** Burden of proof: the covered entity must demonstrate either that all required notifications were made, or that the event didn't meet 164.402's breach definition at all. | Lakeshore, not any regulator, has to prove the negative here — and right now it can't. |

## The actual text

All quotes below come verbatim from `sources/cfr/45-164-breach-notification-excerpt.md`.

### 164.402 — Definitions

> As used in this subpart, the following terms have the following meanings:
> Breach means the acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of protected health information in a
> manner not permitted under subpart E of this part which compromises the security or privacy of
> the protected health information.
> (1) Breach excludes: (i) Any unintentional acquisition, access, or use of protected health
> information by a workforce member or person acting under the authority of a covered entity or a
> business associate, if such acquisition, access, or use was made in good faith and within the
> scope of authority and does not result in further use or disclosure in a manner not permitted
> under subpart E of this part. (ii) Any inadvertent disclosure by a person who is authorized to
> access protected health information at a covered entity or business associate to another person
> authorized to access protected health information at the same covered entity or business
> associate, or organized health care arrangement in which the covered entity participates, and
> the information received as a result of such disclosure is not further used or disclosed in a
> manner not permitted under subpart E of this part. (iii) A disclosure of protected health
> information where a covered entity or business associate has a good faith belief that an
> unauthorized person to whom the disclosure was made would not reasonably have been able to
> retain such information.
> (2) Except as provided in paragraph (1) of this definition, an acquisition, access, use, or
> disclosure of protected health information in a manner not permitted under subpart E is presumed
> to be a breach unless the covered entity or business associate, as applicable, demonstrates that
> there is a low probability that the protected health information has been compromised based on
> a risk assessment of at least the following factors: (i) The nature and extent of the protected
> health information involved, including the types of identifiers and the likelihood of
> re-identification; (ii) The unauthorized person who used the protected health information or to
> whom the disclosure was made; (iii) Whether the protected health information was actually
> acquired or viewed; and (iv) The extent to which the risk to the protected health information has
> been mitigated.
> Unsecured protected health information means protected health information that is not rendered
> unusable, unreadable, or indecipherable to unauthorized persons through the use of a technology
> or methodology specified by the Secretary in the guidance issued under section 13402(h)(2) of
> Public Law 111-5.

The exclusions in (1) read like a checklist for ruling this incident out quickly — and none of
them fit. (i) requires the PHI to have stayed inside Lakeshore's workforce, with no further
exposure; a laptop in a stranger's shared ride is the opposite of that. (ii) requires the
disclosure to land on another person already authorized to see PHI at Lakeshore; nobody knows
who, if anyone, has the laptop. (iii) requires a good-faith belief the recipient couldn't have
retained the information; there's no recipient to have a good-faith belief about, because the
device is simply missing. None of the three narrow doors out apply. That pushes this straight
into 164.402(2)'s presumption — and the four-factor test is the only way out of it.

### 164.404 — Notification to individuals

> (a) Standard—(1) General rule. A covered entity shall, following the discovery of a breach of
> unsecured protected health information, notify each individual whose unsecured protected health
> information has been, or is reasonably believed by the covered entity to have been, accessed,
> acquired, used, or disclosed as a result of such breach.
> (2) Breaches treated as discovered. For purposes of paragraph (a)(1) of this section, §§
> 164.406(a), and 164.408(a), a breach shall be treated as discovered by a covered entity as of the
> first day on which such breach is known to the covered entity, or, by exercising reasonable
> diligence would have been known to the covered entity. A covered entity shall be deemed to have
> knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or by exercising reasonable diligence would have
> been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is a workforce
> member or agent of the covered entity (determined in accordance with the federal common law of
> agency).
> (b) Implementation specification: Timeliness of notification. Except as provided in § 164.412, a
> covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without
> unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.
> (c) Implementation specifications: Content of notification—(1) Elements. The notification
> required by paragraph (a) of this section shall include, to the extent possible: (A) A brief
> description of what happened, including the date of the breach and the date of the discovery of
> the breach, if known; (B) A description of the types of unsecured protected health information
> that were involved in the breach (such as whether full name, social security number, date of
> birth, home address, account number, diagnosis, disability code, or other types of information
> were involved); (C) Any steps individuals should take to protect themselves from potential harm
> resulting from the breach; (D) A brief description of what the covered entity involved is doing
> to investigate the breach, to mitigate harm to individuals, and to protect against any further
> breaches; and (E) Contact procedures for individuals to ask questions or learn additional
> information, which shall include a toll-free telephone number, an e-mail address, Web site, or
> postal address.
> (2) Plain language requirement. The notification required by paragraph (a) of this section shall
> be written in plain language.

Notice (a)(2): the 60-day clock doesn't wait for your own internal investigation to finish or
for a formal breach determination to be signed. It starts the day the incident is known or
reasonably should have been known to any workforce member or agent — which, for this incident,
is the day the laptop was reported missing, not the day this module's four-factor analysis
concludes. 164.412 (law-enforcement delay) is referenced as the sole named exception to that
60-day clock; this course names that the exception exists without describing its mechanics,
since that section hasn't been independently sourced.

### 164.406 — Notification to the media

> (a) Standard. For a breach of unsecured protected health information involving more than 500
> residents of a State or jurisdiction, a covered entity shall, following the discovery of the
> breach as provided in § 164.404(a)(2), notify prominent media outlets serving the State or
> jurisdiction.
> (b) Implementation specification: Timeliness of notification. Except as provided in § 164.412, a
> covered entity shall provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this section without
> unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after discovery of a breach.

### 164.408 — Notification to the Secretary

> (a) Standard. A covered entity shall, following the discovery of a breach of unsecured protected
> health information as provided in § 164.404(a)(2), notify the Secretary.
> (b) Implementation specifications: Breaches involving 500 or more individuals. For breaches of
> unsecured protected health information involving 500 or more individuals, a covered entity
> shall, except as provided in § 164.412, provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of
> this section contemporaneously with the notice required by § 164.404(a) and in the manner
> specified on the HHS Web site.
> (c) Implementation specifications: Breaches involving less than 500 individuals. For breaches of
> unsecured protected health information involving less than 500 individuals, a covered entity
> shall maintain a log or other documentation of such breaches and, not later than 60 days after
> the end of each calendar year, provide the notification required by paragraph (a) of this
> section for breaches discovered during the preceding calendar year, in the manner specified on
> the HHS web site.

### 164.414 — Administrative requirements and burden of proof

> (a) Administrative requirements. A covered entity is required to comply with the administrative
> requirements of § 164.530(b), (d), (e), (g), (h), (i), and (j) with respect to the requirements
> of this subpart.
> (b) Burden of proof. In the event of a use or disclosure in violation of subpart E, the covered
> entity or business associate, as applicable, shall have the burden of demonstrating that all
> notifications were made as required by this subpart or that the use or disclosure did not
> constitute a breach, as defined at § 164.402.

164.414(b) is worth reading twice, because it's the provision that makes "we're still not sure"
an untenable final answer. The burden sits on Lakeshore, not on OCR (the HHS Office for Civil
Rights) or on any donor, to demonstrate one of exactly two things: that it made every
notification this subpart requires, or that the event never met 164.402's breach definition in
the first place. Silence, or an unresolved "maybe," satisfies neither branch.

## Running the four-factor test — honestly, against the real facts

This is the module's actual job. Not citing the test — running it, on the facts this course
has locked, and following the reasoning wherever it leads, even if that's an uncomfortable
answer.

**Factor 1 — nature and extent of the PHI, including re-identification likelihood.** The
extract module 1 locked holds six fields across roughly 212 donors: BECS-internal donor
identifier, donor name, date of birth, each eligibility determination with its date, deferral
reason codes, and lifetime donation count. Name plus date of birth is itself a classic
re-identification pair; paired with an eligibility determination and a deferral code, it's not
abstract health information — it's "this named person, born this date, was deferred from
donating, for this specific reason." That's about as re-identifiable and as sensitive as a
donor-eligibility record gets. This factor does not favor Lakeshore. It weighs toward a
meaningful compromise risk, not a trivial one.

**Factor 2 — who the unauthorized person was, or who the disclosure went to.** Here's the
honest answer: nobody knows. The laptop is lost, not confirmed stolen by an identified actor.
It may be sitting unopened in a rideshare's lost-and-found. It may be in the hands of someone
who has no idea what's on it. It may be in the hands of someone who does. 164.402(2)(ii) asks
specifically who received the disclosure — and this incident simply doesn't have that
fact. An unknown recipient isn't a factor that favors low probability of compromise; at best,
it's neutral, and in practice an unidentified, unaccountable recipient is exactly the scenario
this factor exists to flag as higher-risk, not lower.

**Factor 3 — whether the PHI was actually acquired or viewed. This is where module 3's
encryption gap becomes this module's problem.** If Lakeshore could confirm, device-level, that
full-disk encryption was active on this laptop when it went missing, this factor would do
enormous work toward rebutting the presumption: encrypted data, rendered unreadable to anyone
without the key, is not meaningfully "acquired or viewed" in any sense that matters to a person
whose eligibility record it is. It might also mean the data was never "unsecured protected
health information" under 164.402's own definition at all — potentially closing the question
before the four factors even need weighing.

But that confirmation doesn't exist. Module 3 locked this precisely: the systems administrator
can confirm the device was enrolled under Lakeshore's encryption policy; he cannot confirm
encryption was actually running on it at the moment it went missing, because a
device-management platform migration left this one unit's encryption-status field reading "not
reported" for the exact window that matters. That is not the same as "encryption failed," and
it is not the same as "encryption was confirmed active." It is a genuine, unresolved unknown.

Carry that unknown into this factor honestly: Lakeshore cannot say the PHI was likely not
acquired or viewed, because it cannot say the one thing that would support that conclusion —
that the data was unreadable to begin with. A factor that depends entirely on an unconfirmed
premise cannot be scored in Lakeshore's favor. It has to be scored as unresolved, which, under
a presumption-of-breach standard, functions the same as scored against Lakeshore: an
unrebutted factor doesn't help rebut anything.

**Factor 4 — extent of mitigation.** Some mitigation is real and already in motion: the loss
was reported promptly (164.404(a)(2)'s discovery clock is already running from that report),
Lakeshore's device-management platform is the same central system that enforces the encryption
policy at enrollment, and a platform with that level of fleet control plausibly supports a
remote lock or remote wipe command issued the moment the device was reported missing — a
reasonable mitigation step for a Director to confirm was actually issued, not assume happened
automatically. Against that: the device itself has not been recovered, there is no confirmation
a remote command actually reached it (a lost device that's powered off or offline never
receives a pending remote wipe), and — the same gap running through every factor — encryption
status still cannot be confirmed. Some mitigation steps exist. The one mitigation step that
would matter most here, confirmed encryption, isn't among them.

**The determination, stated precisely, the way this curriculum states every honest finding:**
Factor 1 weighs against Lakeshore (meaningful re-identification risk, sensitive fields).
Factor 2 is unknown, which does not favor low probability of compromise. Factor 3 — the
pivotal factor, because it's the one factor an encryption confirmation could have resolved
decisively in Lakeshore's favor — is genuinely unresolved, not merely unfavorable: Lakeshore
cannot demonstrate the PHI was likely not acquired or viewed, because it cannot demonstrate the
data was rendered unreadable in the first place. Factor 4 shows some real mitigation and one
significant gap. Four factors, and not one of them clearly rebuts the presumption.

164.402(2) does not ask whether Lakeshore *might* be able to show low probability of
compromise eventually. It asks whether Lakeshore can demonstrate that today. **As of right now,
it cannot.** That means this incident must be treated **as a reportable breach**, under
164.402's presumption, **unless and until further investigation changes this picture** — which
is explicitly not this module's job. `investigating-a-healthcare-data-incident` picks up
exactly this open thread: if the systems administrator's investigation later confirms
encryption was active, factor 3 flips, and the determination may reverse. Until that happens,
the presumption stands, and Lakeshore has to act like it stands — not quietly wait for better
facts while the 60-day clock keeps running regardless of where the analysis sits.

## What follows from treating this as a breach, provisionally

Nothing here waits for certainty to finish forming. 164.404(a)(2) started the clock the day the
loss was reported, and 164.414(b) puts the burden of proving otherwise on Lakeshore, not on
anyone else. Here's what a provisional breach determination maps onto right now:

- **Individual notification (164.404).** All roughly 212 affected donors get notified, in plain
  language, within 60 calendar days of discovery — not 60 days from today, 60 days from the day
  the laptop was first reported missing. The notice needs all five content elements: what
  happened and when, what types of PHI were involved (name, date of birth, eligibility
  determination, deferral code — the fields actually in the extract), what the individual can
  do to protect themselves, what Lakeshore is doing to investigate and mitigate, and contact
  procedures. If module 5's investigation later rebuts the presumption, that doesn't un-send a
  notification already required on the facts known when the clock was running — the honest
  path is to notify now, on the current facts, and revise if warranted, not to wait on an
  investigation with no fixed end date while a hard 60-day deadline keeps moving.
- **Media notification (164.406) — not triggered.** The threshold is more than 500 residents of
  a State or jurisdiction. This extract covers roughly 212 donors. Well under the line. No
  media notification is owed here, and it would be a mistake to treat this provision as
  engaged just because a breach presumption stands — the two questions (is it a breach, is it
  big enough to trigger media notice) are genuinely separate, and this incident clears the
  first bar without coming close to the second.
- **HHS notification (164.408) — the under-500 pathway, not the 500-plus pathway.** 164.408(b)
  requires breaches of 500 or more individuals to notify the Secretary *contemporaneously* with
  individual notification. That's not this incident. 164.408(c) is the applicable track: for
  breaches under 500 individuals, Lakeshore maintains a log or other documentation of the
  breach and reports it to the Secretary not later than 60 days after the end of the calendar
  year in which it was discovered — an annual batch filing, not an immediate one. Get this
  distinction right before anyone reflexively files on the 500-plus timeline: filing
  contemporaneously isn't wrong, exactly, but it's not what 164.408(c) requires, and conflating
  the two tracks is its own kind of sloppy compliance.

## The dual-reporting comparison — honestly, not forced

`filing-a-biological-product-deviation-report` already taught 606.171's own reporting
mechanics in full: a two-prong reportability test (a deviation that may affect a distributed
product's safety, purity, or potency) and a 45-calendar-day clock, filed on Form FDA-3486 to
CBER (the FDA's Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research). None of that gets re-derived
here. What's worth putting side by side is the shape of the comparison itself:

| | HIPAA Breach Notification Rule | 606.171 BPDR (Biological Product Deviation Report) |
|---|---|---|
| Triggering test | An impermissible use/disclosure/access/acquisition of PHI, not excluded, with the presumption of breach unrebutted by the four factors | A deviation that may affect the safety, purity, or potency of a *distributed* blood product |
| Clock | 60 calendar days from discovery (164.404(b)) | 45 calendar days from discovery (606.171(c)) |
| Owed to | HHS/OCR, plus affected individuals (and media/HHS-contemporaneous above 500) | FDA/CBER, on Form FDA-3486 |
| What it protects | Confidentiality and privacy of PHI | Product safety, purity, and potency for a patient who may receive the product |

The two clocks are genuinely different lengths, triggered by genuinely different tests, and
owed to different regulators for different reasons. They can both apply to the same real-world
event — but only when that event actually clears both tests independently. **This incident
doesn't.** Per module 1's own locked fact, the ~212 donors in the extract are a clean
population: no connection to any open deviation, CAPA (corrective and preventive action), or
other quality event at Lakeshore. There is no distributed blood product whose safety, purity,
or potency this laptop loss could plausibly affect — it's a privacy-and-security-scoped
incident about a data extract, not a product-quality event about a unit of blood or plasma.
Running 606.171(b)'s own two-prong test against these facts the same honest way module 4 ran
164.402's four factors: there's no deviation here that touches a distributed product at all,
so the test doesn't engage, and **this incident does not independently trigger a BPDR
filing.**

That's the real teaching moment, and it only lands if the lesson doesn't fudge it: a single
incident *could* trigger both clocks at once — for example, if the same lost device had also
carried data tied to a product already under recall, or if the deferral-coding data it held
turned out to reflect an error that also misclassified a *distributed* unit's eligibility
status, raising an independent safety/purity/potency question. Neither of those is true here.
Forcing a BPDR onto an incident that doesn't meet 606.171(b)'s own test, just because this
course is about "dual reporting," would be the opposite of what this curriculum has built its
credibility on. The honest answer is simpler and more useful: know both tests well enough to
run each one on its own facts, recognize when only one applies, and don't file something FDA
never asked for just to look thorough.

## What an inspector or reviewer would actually look for

An OCR investigator reviewing this incident wouldn't start by asking whether Lakeshore
concluded "breach" or "no breach." They'd ask to see the four-factor risk assessment itself —
dated, reasoned, signed, showing the actual analysis, not just a conclusion. A weak answer
sounds like "we didn't think it rose to the level of a breach" with nothing behind it. A
credible answer produces this exact document: factor by factor, what was known, what wasn't,
and why the presumption did or didn't get rebutted. 164.414(b) puts the burden of proof on
Lakeshore — an investigator who asks "prove it wasn't a breach" and gets silence, or a shrug,
has just found the citation. The device-management migration's own status log, showing
"not reported" for this unit, needs to be part of that same record — it's the single piece of
evidence that explains why factor 3 couldn't be resolved in Lakeshore's favor, and an
investigator will want to see that Lakeshore *looked* for that evidence, not that it simply
assumed the policy held.

## Common traps

**"We have a reasonable encryption policy, so this isn't a breach."** This is the trap module
3 built directly into this module's foundation, and it's worth refuting explicitly one more
time: a sound Addressable-specification policy decision under 164.306(d)(3) answers a Security
Rule question. It does not, by itself, answer 164.402's question, which turns on what actually
happened to *this device's* data, not on how reasonable the policy was in general. A policy
can be perfect and a specific device's status can still be unconfirmed — and an unconfirmed
status cannot rebut a presumption.

**"We don't know for sure it's a breach, so we'll wait until we do before notifying anyone."**
This is the trap 164.414(b)'s burden-of-proof standard exists to close. The rule doesn't give a
covered entity a third option of "undetermined, pending further review, clock paused." It gives
two: demonstrate the notifications were made, or demonstrate the event wasn't a breach at all.
"We're still investigating" satisfies neither branch, and the 60-day clock in 164.404(b) keeps
running regardless of how long the internal investigation takes. The honest posture, given a
genuinely unresolved factor 3, is to treat this as a breach now, on the facts in hand, and
revise only if a later investigation produces the confirmation that would actually change the
answer — not to sit on the determination hoping for an answer that makes notification
unnecessary.

## What this means for your job

- **Treat "the presumption wasn't rebutted" as its own clear answer, not a placeholder for
  "we're still deciding."** Under 164.402(2), an unrebutted presumption *is* the determination:
  breach, provisionally, until new facts change it. Don't let your team treat "unresolved" as a
  reason to delay notification — the clock doesn't care that the analysis feels unfinished.
- **Ask which specific factor is actually in question, not just "is this a breach."** This
  incident's whole determination turns on one factor — whether the data was actually readable —
  tied directly to one unresolved fact from a prior module. Knowing that lets you ask your QA
  and your systems administrator the one question that would actually move the needle: can we
  confirm encryption status, yes or no, and how fast can we know.
- **Know which HHS track applies before anyone drafts a filing.** Under 500 individuals means
  the annual-log pathway (164.408(c)), not the contemporaneous one (164.408(b)). Filing on the
  wrong track isn't a compliance win for being "extra careful" — it signals the team doesn't
  actually know which rule applies.
- **Don't let "dual reporting" become "report everything to everyone."** A HIPAA breach and a
  BPDR-reportable deviation are two separate tests on two separate sets of facts. Make your QA
  show you that a distributed-product safety/purity/potency question actually exists before a
  BPDR gets filed alongside a HIPAA notification — filing one because the other is happening is
  itself a finding waiting to happen.
- **Keep the provisional nature of this determination visible to everyone who needs to act on
  it.** Counsel, compliance, and your CIO (Chief Information Officer) all need to hear the same
  sentence: this is being treated as a breach on the facts known today, because the presumption
  hasn't been rebutted — not that it's a closed, final determination.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your systems administrator says, "We can't confirm encryption either way, so let's call this a 50/50 and wait for more facts before deciding anything." Is that how 164.402 works?

No. 164.402(2) doesn't set up a neutral default or a waiting period. It sets a **presumption of
breach** that only goes away if Lakeshore affirmatively demonstrates low probability of
compromise across the four factors. An unresolved factor — here, whether the data was actually
readable — doesn't average out to "undecided." It fails to rebut the presumption, which means
the presumption stands: treat this as a breach, provisionally, on the facts known now. Waiting
indefinitely for more facts isn't a safe middle path; 164.414(b) puts the burden on Lakeshore to
prove otherwise, and the 60-day notification clock in 164.404(b) keeps running the entire time
the team waits.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Does this incident require filing a Biological Product Deviation Report (BPDR) under 606.171, since Lakeshore is already running a HIPAA breach analysis on it?

No — and this is the honest answer, not a convenient one. 606.171(b)'s reportability test asks
whether a deviation may affect the safety, purity, or potency of a *distributed* blood product.
Per module 1's own locked fact, the ~212 donors in this extract are a clean population with no
connection to any open deviation or quality event — there's no distributed product and no
safety/purity/potency question anywhere in this incident's facts. Running HIPAA's breach test
and 606.171's BPDR test are two separate analyses on two separate questions; this incident
clears the first test's presumption-of-breach bar without coming anywhere near the second
test's own trigger. Filing a BPDR here, just because the course is about dual reporting, would
be reporting something FDA never asked for.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: If this breach presumption stands, which HHS notification track applies — the 500-or-more pathway or the under-500 pathway?

The under-500 pathway, 164.408(c). The extract covers roughly 212 donors — well under the
500-individual threshold that triggers 164.408(b)'s *contemporaneous* HHS notification (and
164.406's media notification, which also isn't triggered here). Under 164.408(c), Lakeshore
instead maintains a log or other documentation of the breach and reports it to the Secretary no
later than 60 days after the end of the calendar year in which it was discovered — an annual
batch filing, not an immediate one. Individual notification under 164.404 still runs on its own
60-day-from-discovery clock regardless of which HHS track applies; the two clocks are
independent of each other.
:::

## Where this goes next

The determination this module reaches is deliberately provisional, and it's locked exactly as
stated: as of right now, Lakeshore cannot demonstrate a low probability of compromise, so this
incident is being treated as a reportable breach, with individual notification owed on the
164.404 60-day clock and HHS notification owed on the 164.408(c) under-500 annual-log track —
not because the facts are certain, but because an unrebutted presumption is itself the answer
until new facts arrive. `investigating-a-healthcare-data-incident` is where those new facts get
sought: scoping exactly what was on the device, resolving or honestly leaving open the
encryption-status question module 3 raised and this module couldn't close, re-running this
four-factor assessment if the facts change, and reaching this course's final, closing decision
on an incident that has now touched every HIPAA subpart this curriculum built.
